name: explicit domain and codomain of a function
essential_semantics: A function carries its source and target sets as part of its identity; two formulas with the same rule but different domains are different functions.
rationale: Nearly every analytic theorem has a domain hypothesis; a function represented only by its rule cannot satisfy or violate it.

name: real- and vector-valued functions
essential_semantics: Scalar, vector and matrix valued functions of one or several variables, with arity and value type distinguished.
canonical_example: F : R^n -> R^m
rationale: The multivariate/multivalued shape determines which derivative object (gradient, Jacobian, Hessian) is meaningful.

name: partial function with restricted domain
essential_semantics: A function defined on a subset of its nominal source, with the definedness set recoverable.
canonical_example: log : R -> R defined only on x > 0
rationale: Partiality is not an error condition, it is part of the mathematics; systems that model it only as a runtime exception lose it from the statement.

name: piecewise definition over a partition of the domain
essential_semantics: A function defined by cases with guards, where exhaustiveness and mutual exclusivity of the cases are checkable and the pieces' domains are explicit.
canonical_example: f(x) = x for x >= 0, -x for x < 0
rationale: Piecewise objects are ubiquitous (densities, activation functions, tariffs); overlapping or non-exhaustive cases are silent errors.

name: limit of a function at a point
essential_semantics: A limit is a quantified statement (for all epsilon there exists delta), not an evaluation; one-sided limits are distinguished and existence is a claim.
canonical_example: lim_{x -> 0} sin(x)/x = 1
rationale: The limit is the founding construct of analysis and the canonical alternating-quantifier statement; systems that treat it as a numeric operation lose the claim structure.

name: limit of a sequence, including limits at infinity
essential_semantics: Convergence of an indexed family as n tends to infinity, with divergence and oscillation distinguishable from convergence.
canonical_example: lim_{n -> infinity} (1 + 1/n)^n = e
rationale: Asymptotic statements in probability and numerics are sequence limits; the index domain and the mode of convergence are semantic content.

name: continuity at a point and on a set
essential_semantics: Pointwise continuity and continuity on a set are distinct claims, each with an explicit domain.
canonical_example: f is continuous on [a, b]
rationale: Continuity is the most common hypothesis in analysis theorems; it is a property of a function-on-a-domain, not of a formula.

name: uniform continuity and uniform convergence
essential_semantics: Uniformity is expressed by the position of the existential quantifier relative to the universal one and must be preserved distinctly from the pointwise version.
canonical_example: for all eps exists delta for all x versus for all x for all eps exists delta
rationale: This is the sharpest practical test of quantifier-order fidelity: the two statements differ only in binder order and are genuinely different theorems.

name: derivative with respect to a named variable
essential_semantics: The differentiation variable is explicit, the point of evaluation is distinguished from the derivative function, and differentiability is a claim with a domain.
canonical_example: f'(x) = df/dx, and f'(2) evaluated at a point
rationale: Differentiation is the central operator of applied mathematics, and the derivative-as-function versus derivative-at-a-point distinction is frequently collapsed.

name: partial derivative with held-constant variables
essential_semantics: Which variables are held fixed is part of the meaning, not a convention; the same symbol can denote different partials under different variable sets.
canonical_example: (partial f / partial x) at fixed y
rationale: In thermodynamics and economics the held-constant set is written explicitly precisely because omitting it changes the quantity.

name: gradient
essential_semantics: Vector (or covector) of partials with shape determined by the domain, and its distinction from the total derivative recorded.
canonical_example: grad f(x) in R^n for f : R^n -> R
rationale: Optimisation and learning are gradient-driven; shape and variance errors here propagate silently.

name: Jacobian matrix
essential_semantics: Matrix of first partials of a vector-valued function with shape m x n determined by the types.
canonical_example: J_F(x) in R^{m x n} for F : R^n -> R^m
rationale: Change of variables for densities and the multivariate chain rule both require the Jacobian with correct orientation.

name: Hessian and second-order structure
essential_semantics: Matrix of second partials, symmetric under continuity hypotheses, connected to convexity and to optimality conditions.
canonical_example: H f(x) positive semidefinite characterises local convexity
rationale: Second-order conditions and Fisher information are Hessians; symmetry requires a hypothesis that should not be assumed silently.

name: directional and total derivative
essential_semantics: Derivative along a direction, and the total (Frechet) derivative as a linear map, distinguished from the collection of partials.
canonical_example: D_v f(x) = lim_{t->0} (f(x + tv) - f(x))/t
rationale: Existence of all partials does not imply differentiability; systems that identify them are stating something false.

name: higher-order derivatives and smoothness classes
essential_semantics: Derivatives of order k with C^k / C^infinity / analytic smoothness classes as hypotheses.
canonical_example: f in C^2([a,b])
rationale: Smoothness class is the hypothesis of most approximation theorems; treating 'differentiable' as a Boolean loses the order.

name: composition and the chain rule
essential_semantics: Differentiation of composed maps respecting order and shapes, including the matrix-product form in the multivariate case.
canonical_example: D(g o f)(x) = Dg(f(x)) Df(x)
rationale: Backpropagation and change-of-variables are the chain rule; the non-commutative product order is where implementations go wrong.

name: implicit function and implicit differentiation
essential_semantics: Derivatives of a relation-defined function, with the non-degeneracy condition of the implicit function theorem attached.
canonical_example: from x^2 + y^2 = 1, dy/dx = -x/y for y != 0
rationale: Constrained sensitivity analysis relies on it, and its side condition is exactly the sort of thing routinely dropped.

name: derivative with respect to a function
essential_semantics: Variation of a functional with respect to its function argument, distinguished from partials with respect to scalars.
canonical_example: delta S / delta y for an action functional S[y]
rationale: Calculus of variations, physics and variational inference all differentiate with respect to functions, not numbers.

name: definite integral with explicit variable and domain
essential_semantics: Integration binds a variable, carries an explicit domain and an explicit measure/differential; the bound variable does not escape.
canonical_example: integral from 0 to 1 of x^2 dx
rationale: Integration is a binder with a domain and a measure; representations that keep only the integrand lose most of the statement.

name: antiderivative and constant of integration
essential_semantics: The antiderivative is a family of functions differing by a constant, not a single function.
canonical_example: integral of 2x dx = x^2 + C
rationale: Dropping the constant of integration is a small but real loss of the solution family.

name: iterated and multiple integration
essential_semantics: Integration over multidimensional regions with the region description and the order of integration explicit.
canonical_example: double integral over the unit disc of f(x,y) dA
rationale: Marginalisation is a multiple integral; the region and integration order carry Fubini-type side conditions.

name: improper integrals and convergence conditions
essential_semantics: Integrals over unbounded domains or of unbounded integrands are limits, whose existence is a claim.
canonical_example: integral from 1 to infinity of 1/x^2 dx converges; of 1/x diverges
rationale: Normalisability of densities and existence of moments are improper-integral convergence claims.

name: integration over curves and surfaces
essential_semantics: Integration along a parameterised curve or over an embedded surface with orientation recorded.
canonical_example: line integral of F . dr along a closed curve C
rationale: Vector calculus and physics need orientation-aware integration, which a plain domain-integral cannot express.

name: measure
essential_semantics: A countably additive non-negative set function on a sigma-algebra, with the reference measure of an integral nameable.
canonical_example: Lebesgue measure on R; counting measure on N
rationale: Densities are densities with respect to a measure; suppressing the reference measure makes discrete/continuous unification impossible.

name: sigma-algebra of measurable sets
essential_semantics: A collection closed under complement and countable union, usable as an object (for conditioning, filtrations, measurability).
canonical_example: the Borel sigma-algebra on R
rationale: Conditioning on a sigma-algebra and information filtrations are inexpressible without it; this is a hard boundary for probabilistic IRs.

name: measurable function
essential_semantics: Preimages of measurable sets are measurable; measurability is a hypothesis attached to a function and a pair of sigma-algebras.
canonical_example: X : Omega -> R is F/Borel measurable
rationale: A random variable IS a measurable function; systems that define random variables purely by their distribution cannot state measurability.

name: integration against a general measure
essential_semantics: Integral of a measurable function with respect to a named measure, unifying sums and Riemann integrals.
canonical_example: integral of f dmu over A
rationale: It is the construct that lets discrete and continuous cases share one statement; without it they must be duplicated.

name: almost-everywhere / almost-sure qualification
essential_semantics: A property holding outside a null set, with the qualification attached to the statement rather than dropped.
canonical_example: f = g almost everywhere with respect to Lebesgue measure
rationale: The difference between 'everywhere' and 'almost everywhere' is a genuine weakening; a system that drops the qualifier overstates the claim.

name: infinite series and convergence
essential_semantics: An infinite sum is a limit of partial sums; convergence, absolute convergence and conditional convergence are distinguished.
canonical_example: sum_{n=1}^{infinity} 1/n^2 = pi^2/6
rationale: Rearrangement is invalid for conditionally convergent series; a representation that treats infinite sums as finite ones is unsound.

name: distinct modes of convergence
essential_semantics: Pointwise, uniform, L^p, almost-everywhere convergence are separate relations and must not be merged into a single 'converges'.
canonical_example: f_n -> f in L^2 but not pointwise
rationale: Different modes support different theorems; collapsing them is a substantive semantic loss with practical consequences.

name: power series and radius of convergence
essential_semantics: Series in powers of (x - a) with a centre and a radius of convergence carried with it.
canonical_example: sum x^n/n! with infinite radius of convergence
rationale: A series expansion without its region of validity is a common source of misuse outside the radius.

name: Taylor expansion with remainder
essential_semantics: Finite expansion plus an explicit remainder or error term, not an unqualified equality.
rationale: Writing a truncated expansion with '=' rather than '≈ with remainder R' is a textbook example of dropped semantics.

name: asymptotic order notation
essential_semantics: Big-O, little-o, Theta and asymptotic equivalence with the limit point and the variable made explicit; O(.) is a relation, not a value.
canonical_example: f(n) = O(n log n) as n -> infinity
rationale: The '=' in O-notation is not equality; representing it as such licenses invalid symmetric reasoning.

name: ordinary differential equation
essential_semantics: A relation among a function and its derivatives with the independent variable, the unknown function and the order identified.
canonical_example: y'' + omega^2 y = 0
rationale: Dynamics is expressed as differential equations; the unknown being a function rather than a number is the key typing fact.

name: partial differential equation
essential_semantics: Relation among partial derivatives of a multivariate unknown function, with the independent variables and domain explicit.
canonical_example: u_t = alpha u_xx on (0, L) x (0, T)
rationale: The spatial domain and boundary data are as much a part of the problem as the equation; keeping only the equation is a lossy representation.

name: initial condition
essential_semantics: Value of the unknown (and derivatives) at a specified point, attached to the differential equation as part of one problem object.
rationale: Without initial data the solution is a family; conflating the equation with the initial-value problem loses well-posedness.

name: boundary condition with type
essential_semantics: Dirichlet, Neumann, Robin and periodic conditions distinguished, attached to a specified part of the boundary.
canonical_example: u = 0 on the boundary (Dirichlet)
rationale: Boundary-condition type determines solution existence and uniqueness; an untyped 'boundary value' is insufficient.

name: variational / stationarity problem over functions
essential_semantics: Extremising a functional over an admissible class of functions with the class stated.
canonical_example: minimise integral of L(y, y') dx over y with y(a)=A, y(b)=B
rationale: The admissible class is where the boundary conditions and regularity live; dropping it makes the problem ill-posed.

name: function spaces as typed objects
essential_semantics: L^p, C^k, Sobolev and Hilbert spaces as types with their norm and equivalence relation, so membership is a checkable hypothesis.
rationale: Statements in functional analysis, signal processing and nonparametric statistics quantify over function spaces.

name: metric and metric-space structure
essential_semantics: A distance function with its axioms, generalising absolute value, and the induced notions of ball and convergence.
canonical_example: d(x,y) = |x - y| on R
rationale: Convergence and continuity outside R^n need an explicit metric; assuming Euclidean distance is an unrecorded commitment.

name: supremum and infimum versus maximum and minimum
essential_semantics: Least upper bound of a set, possibly not attained and possibly infinite, distinguished from a maximum.
canonical_example: sup of (0,1) is 1 but has no maximum
rationale: Optimisation statements that say 'min' where only 'inf' is justified assert attainment that may be false.

name: monotonicity, boundedness and convexity of functions
essential_semantics: Qualitative function properties as stated, checkable predicates with a domain.
canonical_example: f is non-decreasing on [0, infinity)
rationale: CDFs, utility functions and objectives are characterised by such properties; they are part of the mathematical content, not metadata.

name: holomorphy, poles and residues
essential_semantics: Complex differentiability with singularity classification and contour integration.
canonical_example: residue of 1/(z^2+1) at z = i
rationale: Characteristic functions and transform inversion rely on complex analysis; without it those results are opaque.

name: integral transforms
essential_semantics: Fourier, Laplace, Mellin and related transforms as operators on functions, with the convention (sign, 2 pi placement) recorded.
canonical_example: F(omega) = integral f(t) e^{-i omega t} dt
rationale: Transform conventions differ across fields; an unrecorded convention makes results incomparable.

name: convolution
essential_semantics: A binary operation on functions or measures with its own domain conditions, distinguished from pointwise product.
canonical_example: (f * g)(x) = integral f(y) g(x - y) dy
rationale: The distribution of a sum of independent random variables is a convolution; representing it as multiplication is wrong.

name: generalized functions / Schwartz distributions
essential_semantics: Objects such as the Dirac delta defined by their action on test functions, and explicitly not ordinary functions.
canonical_example: integral delta(x) phi(x) dx = phi(0)
rationale: Included partly because 'distribution' is dangerously overloaded between analysis and probability; a good IR keeps them distinct.

name: named special functions with branch and domain data
essential_semantics: Gamma, Beta, Bessel, erf, log with their domains, poles and branch cuts recorded rather than assumed.
canonical_example: Gamma(n) = (n-1)! for positive integers, with poles at non-positive integers
rationale: Normalising constants of standard distributions are special functions; branch and domain data is real semantic content.

name: fixed points and contraction
essential_semantics: Solutions of x = T(x) with contraction or compactness hypotheses making existence a theorem rather than an assumption.
canonical_example: a contraction on a complete metric space has a unique fixed point
rationale: Equilibrium concepts and iterative schemes are fixed-point statements; the hypotheses are what make them valid.
